transcript.heading: News Report One (British Female)
paras: A new study has found that eating breakfast every day is associated with better academic performance in children and teenagers, according to researchers at the University of Iowa. The study analyzed data from over 5,000 middle school students and found that those who ate breakfast regularly scored significantly higher on standardized tests in math, reading, and science compared to those who skipped breakfast. Researchers say that breakfast provides essential nutrients and energy that the brain needs to function well, and that hungry students have more difficulty concentrating and retaining information. The study also found that the quality of breakfast matters—students who ate nutritious breakfasts with protein, whole grains, and fruit performed better than those who ate sugary, processed breakfasts.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: Amsterdam has announced plans to ban the sale of gasoline and diesel-powered cars and motorcycles within the city by 2030, making it one of the first major cities in the world to phase out fossil fuel vehicles. The plan, which was approved by the city council, will gradually restrict the use of polluting vehicles in the city center, with the goal of having only zero-emission vehicles by 2030. The city will invest in expanding electric vehicle charging infrastructure and improving public transportation and cycling facilities to support the transition. Amsterdam already has one of the highest rates of cycling in the world, and city officials say that the ban will help improve air quality and reduce noise pollution, making the city healthier and more livable for residents.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: Researchers at MIT have developed a new type of robot that can self-reconfigure, changing its shape and function depending on the task. The robot is made up of small, identical modular units that can attach and detach from each other, allowing the robot to transform into different configurations—like a snake for crawling through tight spaces, a wheel for rolling, or a four-legged walker for navigating rough terrain. The modules communicate with each other wirelessly and can reorganize autonomously without human intervention. Researchers say that these self-reconfiguring robots could be useful in situations where the environment is unpredictable, such as search and rescue operations, space exploration, or construction in challenging environments. The technology is still in the experimental stage, but researchers are working to make the modules smaller and more capable.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Mia): Hey Alex, I need your help. I'm looking for a new apartment, and I'm feeling really overwhelmed.
Man (Alex): Oh no, apartment hunting is the worst. What's going on? Are you moving out of your current place?
Woman: Yeah, my lease is up at the end of next month, and my landlord is raising the rent by $300. I can't afford that, so I need to find somewhere new.
Man: Ugh, that's frustrating. Rent is so expensive these days. What's your budget?
Woman: I'd like to stay under $1,500 a month, including utilities if possible. But I know that might be unrealistic in this city.
Man: Yeah, $1,500 is pretty tight. But it's not impossible, especially if you're willing to look a bit further from the city center. What are you looking for in an apartment?

Woman: Well, I need at least one bedroom, and I'd prefer a place with a decent kitchen since I like to cook. A dishwasher would be amazing, but I know that's a luxury. And I'd like to be close to public transportation since I don't have a car.
Man: Those are reasonable requirements. Have you started looking online?

Woman: Yeah, I've been checking Zillow and Craigslist, but it's so overwhelming. There are so many listings, and a lot of them look too good to be true. And every time I find something I like, it's already rented by the time I contact the landlord.
Man: I know the feeling. The market moves really fast. You have to be ready to act quickly. Have you considered getting a roommate? That would allow you to afford a nicer place or a better location.
Woman: I've thought about it, but I've lived alone for the past three years and I really value my privacy. I'm not sure I'm ready to have a roommate again.
Man: That's understandable. What about neighborhoods? Do you have a specific area in mind?
Woman: I'd like to stay in the same general area—close to the park and the cafes I like. But I'm open to other neighborhoods if they're safe and have good transit access.

Man: Have you checked out the neighborhood near the university? There are a lot of apartment buildings there, and rents tend to be a bit cheaper because there's so much supply. It's also well-served by public transit.
Woman: I haven't really looked there. I always assumed it was mostly student housing, which can be noisy.
Man: Some of it is, but there are also regular apartment buildings that aren't just for students. And it's actually a nice area—lots of restaurants and shops, and it's close to the river.
Woman: Hmm, that's worth considering. Do you have any other tips? I've never had to apartment hunt before.

Man: A few things. First, make sure you have all your documents ready—proof of income, references, a credit report. Landlords want to move fast, so if you're prepared, you'll have an advantage. Second, don't be afraid to ask questions—about utilities, parking, laundry, pet policies, whatever. And third, trust your gut. If a place feels off, it probably is.
Woman: Those are good tips. What about scams? I've heard there are a lot of fake listings on Craigslist.

Man: Yeah, you have to be careful. If a listing seems too good to be true, it probably is. Never send money before seeing the apartment in person, and be wary of landlords who are out of the country or who pressure you to act immediately.
Woman: Okay, that's good to know. Thanks for all the advice, Alex. I feel a little less stressed now.
Man: No problem! And if you want, I can come with you to look at apartments. A second pair of eyes is always helpful.
Woman: Really? That would be great. I'd really appreciate that.
Man: Of course. Just let me know when you have some viewings scheduled.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

9. What is Mia's budget?
10. What neighborhood does Alex suggest?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Leo): Hey Sophie, I saw a picture of a painting you posted on Instagram. Did you paint that?
Woman (Sophie): Yeah, I did! I've been getting into painting lately as a hobby. It's been really fun.
Man: That's awesome! I had no idea you painted. How long have you been doing it?
Woman: Only about six months. I took a beginner's class at the community center, and I've been hooked ever since. I mostly paint landscapes and still life.
Man: Six months? That's impressive—it looks really good. I've always wanted to learn to paint, but I have zero artistic talent. I can barely draw a stick figure.
Woman: Oh, come on. Painting isn't about talent—it's about practice. Everyone starts somewhere. You should try it!
Man: I don't know. I tried art class in high school and was terrible at it. My paintings always ended up looking like a mess.
Woman: That's because you were probably trying to make it perfect. Painting is about the process, not the result. It's supposed to be relaxing and fun, not stressful.
Man: Hmm, maybe. But I'm so used to being good at things that it's hard to do something I'm bad at.
Woman: I totally get that. But that's exactly why you should try it! It's good to step outside your comfort zone. And painting is really therapeutic—it helps me de-stress after a long week.
Man: What kind of painting do you do? Acrylic? Oil? Watercolor?

Woman: I started with acrylics because they're beginner-friendly—they dry fast and you can paint over mistakes easily. But I've been experimenting with watercolors lately too. They're more challenging because you can't really fix mistakes, but I love how they look.
Man: That sounds complicated. Do I need to buy a lot of expensive supplies to start?

Woman: Not at all! For beginners, you just need some basic acrylic paints, a few brushes, a canvas or some paper, and maybe a palette. You can get a starter kit for like $20. You don't need anything fancy.
Man: That's more affordable than I thought. Where do you paint? Do you have a studio?
Woman: Ha, I wish! I just paint at my kitchen table. I put down an old tablecloth to protect the surface, and that's my "studio." It's not fancy, but it works.
Man: That's actually really inspiring. Maybe I should give it a try. Do you have any tips for a complete beginner?

Woman: Yeah! Start with something simple, like a still life of fruit or a basic landscape. Don't try to paint a portrait or something complicated right away. And don't be afraid to make mistakes—that's how you learn. Also, watch some beginner tutorials on YouTube—there are tons of free ones that are really helpful.
Man: Those are good tips. Maybe I'll pick up a starter kit this weekend.
Woman: You should! And if you want, we could paint together sometime. I can show you some basic techniques.
Man: That would be really fun. Let's do it. Thanks for the encouragement, Sophie.
Woman: No problem! I think you'll love it once you get started.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Female)
paras: The Industrial Revolution was one of the most transformative periods in human history, changing nearly every aspect of daily life and laying the foundation for the modern world. Beginning in Britain in the late 18th century and spreading throughout Europe and North America over the next century, the Industrial Revolution shifted economies from agrarian and handcraft-based to industrial and machine-based.

Before the Industrial Revolution, most people lived in rural areas and worked in agriculture or cottage industries, where goods were produced by hand in people's homes. The invention of new machines—like the spinning jenny, the power loom, and most importantly, the steam engine—revolutionized production. Factories emerged, bringing workers and machines together under one roof and dramatically increasing output. The steam engine, perfected by James Watt in the 1770s, was particularly important because it could power factories, trains, and ships, freeing industry from dependence on water power and enabling factories to be built anywhere.

The Industrial Revolution had profound social consequences. Millions of people moved from rural areas to cities, causing rapid urbanization. Cities grew at an unprecedented rate, often without proper infrastructure, leading to overcrowding, poor sanitation, and widespread disease. Factory work was harsh—workers, including children, labored for 12 to 16 hours a day in dangerous conditions for low wages. Labor movements and government regulations eventually led to improved working conditions and the establishment of workers' rights.

The economic impact was equally significant. Mass production made goods cheaper and more widely available, raising the standard of living for many people over time. A new middle class of factory owners, merchants, and professionals emerged, while the working class grew dramatically. The Industrial Revolution also spurred innovation in transportation—canals, railways, and steamships connected markets and made trade faster and cheaper.

The environmental consequences were severe. Coal burning for factories and heating caused massive air pollution in industrial cities, and factories dumped waste into rivers, causing water pollution. Deforestation and resource extraction increased dramatically. Many of the environmental challenges we face today, including climate change, have their roots in the Industrial Revolution's reliance on fossil fuels.

Despite its many problems, the Industrial Revolution set the stage for modern technological progress and economic growth. It transformed agriculture, manufacturing, transportation, and communication, and it fundamentally changed how people lived and worked. The effects of the Industrial Revolution continue to shape our world today.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Male)
paras: Bees and other pollinators play a crucial role in ecosystems and agriculture, yet their populations are declining worldwide at an alarming rate. Pollinators—including bees, butterflies, birds, bats, and beetles—help plants reproduce by transferring pollen from one flower to another. Without them, many plants, including important food crops, would not be able to produce fruits and seeds.

It's estimated that about 75 percent of the world's food crops depend at least in part on pollinators, and that pollinators contribute billions of dollars to the global economy each year. Foods like apples, almonds, blueberries, coffee, and chocolate all rely on pollinators. Beyond agriculture, pollinators are essential for maintaining biodiversity—they help reproduce the wild plants that form the base of many food chains and provide habitat and food for countless other species.

Unfortunately, pollinator populations are declining due to a combination of factors. Habitat loss is a major cause—as natural areas are converted to agriculture, housing, and roads, pollinators lose the flowers they feed on and the places they nest. Pesticide use is another significant factor, particularly neonicotinoid pesticides, which are toxic to bees and can impair their navigation and reproduction. Climate change is also taking a toll, as shifting temperatures and rainfall patterns disrupt the timing of flower blooming and pollinator activity, causing mismatches between when flowers bloom and when pollinators are active. Disease and parasites, such as the varroa mite that affects honeybees, also contribute to population declines.

The decline of pollinators has serious implications for food security, biodiversity, and the economy. Without sufficient pollinators, crop yields could drop, leading to higher food prices and reduced availability of nutritious foods. The loss of wild plant species could cascade through ecosystems, affecting other wildlife.

There are many things that can be done to help pollinators. Planting native flowers and creating pollinator-friendly gardens provides food and habitat. Reducing pesticide use, especially neonicotinoids, helps protect pollinators from toxic exposure. Preserving natural areas and creating corridors of habitat between fragmented landscapes allows pollinators to move and forage more effectively. Supporting organic and sustainable farming practices also helps.

Individuals can make a difference too. Even planting a few flowering plants in a window box or balcony can provide food for pollinators. Buying organic produce supports farming practices that are better for pollinators. And spreading awareness about the importance of pollinators helps build support for conservation efforts.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Volunteering—donating your time and skills to help others without expecting payment—is a rewarding activity that benefits both the people being helped and the volunteers themselves. While many people volunteer because they want to make a difference in their communities, research has shown that volunteering also has significant benefits for physical and mental health, social connection, and even career development.

One of the most well-documented benefits of volunteering is its positive effect on mental health. Studies have found that people who volunteer regularly report lower levels of stress, depression, and anxiety, and higher levels of life satisfaction and happiness. Helping others releases endorphins, the brain's "feel-good" chemicals, and creates a sense of purpose and meaning. Volunteering also provides social connection, reducing loneliness and isolation, which are major risk factors for poor health and early mortality.

Physical health benefits have also been observed. People who volunteer tend to have lower blood pressure, better physical functioning, and even longer lifespans compared to non-volunteers. This may be because volunteering often involves physical activity, and because the social connection and reduced stress have positive effects on the body. Studies have found that adults over 65 who volunteer regularly have better mobility and are less likely to develop high blood pressure than those who don't.

Volunteering can also benefit your career. It provides opportunities to develop new skills, gain work experience, and build your professional network. For people who are changing careers or re-entering the workforce, volunteering can fill gaps in a resume and demonstrate initiative and commitment. Even for people who are happily employed, volunteering can develop leadership skills, teamwork abilities, and other transferable skills that are valuable in the workplace.

There are many different ways to volunteer, so it's important to find something that matches your interests, skills, and schedule. You can volunteer at a local food bank, animal shelter, hospital, school, or community center. You can mentor a young person, help build houses with organizations like Habitat for Humanity, or volunteer at a community garden. Many organizations also offer virtual volunteering opportunities, allowing you to help from home.

It's important to find a volunteer opportunity that's meaningful to you and that fits your lifestyle. You don't need to commit to a huge amount of time—even a few hours a month can make a difference. The key is to find something you enjoy and that aligns with your values.

While volunteering is ultimately about helping others, the benefits to the volunteer are substantial. It's a win-win situation: communities get the help they need, and volunteers get healthier, happier, and more connected in the process.
